title: Routing Basics
description: Understand how ASP.NET Core routing maps incoming URLs to controller actions. Learn about route templates, default values, optional parameters, and the default route pattern used in MVC applications.

blocks.text: **Routing** is the mechanism that maps an incoming URL to the code that should handle it. When a user types `https://yourapp.com/products/details/5` into their browser, the routing system figures out that the `ProductsController.Details(5)` action should handle this request.
Routing sits at the heart of every ASP.NET Core application. Understanding how it works lets you design clean, predictable URLs that are easy for users to remember and for search engines to index.

Routing is configured in `Program.cs` using the `MapControllerRoute` method. When a request arrives, the routing middleware parses the URL and matches it against the defined route patterns. When a match is found, the matched values (like controller name and action name) are used to invoke the correct controller action.

blocks.title: The routing process step by step
items: A browser sends a GET request to `/products/details/5`
The routing middleware parses the URL segments: `products`, `details`, `5`
The default route pattern `{controller=Home}/{action=Index}/{id?}` is matched
ASP.NET Core creates an instance of `ProductsController` and calls `Details(5)`
The action processes the request and returns a response

blocks.text: The MVC template adds a default route in `Program.cs`. This route is the backbone of convention-based routing.

blocks.title: Default route configuration
blocks.content: The default route pattern maps URL segments to controller, action, and an optional id parameter.

blocks.text: Let us break down this pattern. `{controller=Home}` means the first URL segment maps to the controller name, with `Home` as the default. `{action=Index}` means the second segment maps to the action name, defaulting to `Index`. `{id?}` means the third segment is an optional parameter called `id` — the `?` makes it optional.

blocks.title: How different URLs match the default route

blocks.text: Route parameters can have default values and be optional. A default value is used when the URL segment is missing. An optional parameter (marked with `?`) means the route still matches even if that segment is not provided.

blocks.title: Custom route with defaults
blocks.content: Define a route with default values for controller, action, and a custom optional parameter.

blocks.title: Where defaults go
blocks.text: You can provide defaults either inline in the pattern (`{controller=Home}`) or via the `defaults` parameter. Both approaches work. Inline is more concise; the `defaults` object is useful when defaults are complex objects.

Route constraints restrict what values a route parameter can accept. For example, you might want `{id}` to only match integers, or `{year}` to only match four-digit numbers. Constraints prevent ambiguous matches and provide early validation.

blocks.title: Route with int constraint
blocks.content: Add :int to ensure the id parameter only matches numeric values.

blocks.text: With the `int` constraint, a request to `/Products/abc` will not match this route and will result in a 404, rather than passing `abc` as a string and causing a model binding error. We cover constraints in detail in the next lesson.
When you have multiple routes, ASP.NET Core evaluates them in the order they are registered. The first matching route wins. This means more specific routes should come before more general ones.

blocks.title: Route registration order
items: Register the catch-all default route last (e.g., `{controller}/{action}/{id?}`)

blocks.title: Ambiguous routes cause 404s
blocks.text: If two routes could match the same URL, only the first one registered will be used. Make sure your routes are ordered from most specific to most general to avoid requests silently matching the wrong route.

Rather than hardcoding URLs in your views (e.g., `<a href="/Products/Details/5">`), you should generate URLs from route names. This way, if you change a route pattern later, all generated URLs update automatically.

blocks.title: Generating URLs with Url.Action
blocks.content: Use Url.Action in a view or controller to generate a URL based on route names and parameters.
blocks.code: View Product 5 Home

terms.definition: A pattern that maps an incoming URL to a controller action. Routes are registered in Program.cs using MapControllerRoute.
The URL pattern string (e.g., "{controller=Home}/{action=Index}/{id?}") that defines how URLs are parsed and matched.
A placeholder in a route template (e.g., {id}) that captures a value from the URL and passes it to the action method.
A rule applied to a route parameter (e.g., :int, :guid) that restricts what values the parameter can match.
Routing based on URL patterns defined centrally in Program.cs, as opposed to attribute routing which defines routes on individual controllers.

blocks.title: Explore the Default Route
blocks.description: Understand how the default route maps URLs to controllers by testing various URL patterns against your application.
steps: Open Program.cs and locate the MapControllerRoute call with the "default" route name
Note the route pattern, defaults, and any constraints
Run the app and visit `/` — confirm it loads the Home page (HomeController.Index)
Visit `/Home/About` — confirm it loads the About page (HomeController.About)
Visit `/Products` — confirm a 404 (since ProductsController does not exist yet)
Add a new ProductsController with an Index action
Visit `/Products` again and confirm it now loads the Products page
blocks.expectedOutcome: You understand how the default route pattern maps URL segments to controller and action names, and you can predict which action handles any given URL.

blocks.title: Lesson Summary
points: Routing maps incoming URLs to controller actions using route templates
Optional parameters use the `?` suffix — the route still matches if the segment is missing
Default values (e.g., `{controller=Home}`) specify what to use when a segment is absent
Routes are evaluated in registration order — first match wins
Use Url.Action or Url.RouteUrl to generate URLs dynamically instead of hardcoding paths
blocks.takeaway: Routing is the URL-to-code mapping system that connects browser requests to your controller actions. Mastering routing basics gives you precise control over your application's URL structure and ensures users can reach every part of your app.
